subject: Religionskunskap 1
title: Religion, gender and identity
sourceSummary: How religious traditions have historically and today related to gender, examples of religious feminist thinking, religion and sexual identity, and the diversity of interpretations within one and the same religion.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes how religious traditions relate to gender and gender roles, from a religious studies perspective?
questions.opener: Consider whether there is a single, clear-cut "religious view of gender", or whether it varies between traditions, currents and time.
choices: All religions have always had exactly the same view of gender and gender roles, without change over time
The view of gender and gender roles varies between and within religious traditions, and has changed historically, often in interplay with the surrounding society
Religion never has any connection to how gender and gender roles are perceived in a society
Only one religion in the world has ever had male religious leaders
questions.explanation: Research in religious studies shows that the view of gender and gender roles varies both between religions and within one and the same religion, and that it has changed historically in interplay with the wider society. Claiming a single, unchanging "religious view" of gender oversimplifies a considerably more complex reality.

questions.prompt: What characterises religious feminism as a phenomenon, for example Christian or Islamic feminism?
questions.opener: Consider that feminist criticism can come both from outside a religion and from within it, with reference to its own sources.
choices: That one leaves one's religious tradition entirely in order to be a feminist
That one, based on one's own religious tradition's texts, history and theology, argues for equality and questions interpretations held to have disadvantaged women
That all religious feminists agree on exactly the same questions and interpretations
That religious feminism only exists within a single religion
questions.explanation: Religious feminism, for example Christian or Islamic feminism, usually proceeds from the tradition's own texts and theological resources to argue for equality, and questions interpretations considered to have disadvantaged women, rather than leaving the tradition. Religious feminism exists across several different religions and, like other theological currents, contains an internal diversity of positions.

questions.prompt: Within several religious traditions there are differing views on whether women can hold religious leadership positions, for example as priest or imam. What does this say about religious traditions?
questions.opener: Consider whether a single question about leadership can be answered in one single way "for the whole religion".
choices: That the question is always answered identically within a religion, regardless of denomination or country
That there is an internal diversity of interpretations within the same religion, where different denominations, communities or theological schools can reach different conclusions on the same question
That women have never, ever held religious leadership roles in any religion
That the question of leadership is irrelevant to religious studies analysis
questions.explanation: The question of female religious leadership is answered differently within different denominations of the same religion, for example between different Christian communities, which shows the considerable internal diversity of interpretation that exists within every world religion. It is therefore misleading to speak of "the religion's view" on a question as if it were uniform.

questions.prompt: How do religious traditions relate to questions of sexual identity, from a religious studies perspective?
questions.opener: Consider that this is an area with a wide spread of views, both between and within religions.
choices: Exactly the same way within all religions and denominations, without any variation

In highly varied ways: within and between religious traditions there is everything from communities that fully welcome LGBTQ people to more restrictive interpretations, and the debate often continues within the traditions themselves
Religion and questions of sexual identity have historically never intersected
All religious communities have always had identical rules on the question, fixed forever
questions.explanation: Views on sexual identity vary greatly both between and within religious traditions: some communities and theological currents welcome and marry same-sex couples, while others hold to more restrictive interpretations, and the question is often debated vigorously within the traditions themselves. A religious studies description must therefore capture this diversity rather than describing "the religion's position" as uniform.

questions.prompt: A student writes that "Islam oppresses women" as a universal statement. What is the most important religious studies objection to such a statement?
questions.opener: Consider whether the statement takes into account the diversity of interpretations, countries and individual experiences within a global religion.
choices: The statement is correct and needs no nuance

The statement generalises a single interpretation to apply to an entire, global religion with billions of adherents and great internal diversity in terms of culture, legislation, denomination and individual interpretation
The question of gender is entirely irrelevant to Islamic studies
All Muslim women share exactly the same view on the question
questions.explanation: A religious studies way of responding to such a statement is to point out that it generalises a global religion, with enormous variation between countries, cultures, denominations and individual interpretations, based on a single, often oversimplified picture. A careful analysis distinguishes between religious texts, specific interpretive traditions, cultural customs and individual states' legislation, all of which can differ.

questions.prompt: What is an example of a religious studies argument that religious feminists often put forward?
questions.opener: Consider whether the criticism is directed at the religion's sources themselves, or at how the sources have historically been interpreted by (mostly) men.
choices: That sacred texts must always be read exactly literally, without interpretation

That several unequal interpretations do not necessarily follow directly from the sacred sources themselves, but rather from historical, male-dominated interpretive traditions, and that the texts can therefore be read in new ways
That religion and feminism are always completely incompatible
That only a single interpretation of a religious text is ever possible
questions.explanation: A common argument within religious feminism is that many unequal interpretations were shaped by historical, often male-dominated, interpretive traditions rather than by the sacred sources themselves, and that a renewed reading of the texts can make room for a more equal interpretation. This differs from the claim that texts can only be read in a single, literal way.

questions.prompt: Explain, with a concrete example, why it is misleading to speak of "the Christian view of female priesthood" as if it were a single, clear-cut position.
questions.opener: Start from the fact that Christianity contains several major denominations, and compare how they relate to the question.
questions.answer: Within the Church of Sweden and several other Protestant communities, women have been able to be ordained as priests since the mid-20th century, and female priesthood is an established practice there. Within the Roman Catholic Church, by contrast, the priesthood is reserved for men, a position the Church's leadership holds is based on a centuries-long interpretive tradition. Within the Orthodox Church, similarly, the priesthood is reserved for men. At the same time, there are theologians and movements within both Catholic and Orthodox contexts who argue for change. Speaking of "the Christian view" as if it were a single position therefore obscures the considerable difference between Christian denominations, as well as the internal discussions taking place within each of them. A more precise religious studies description therefore always specifies which denomination, which community or which time period a statement concerns.
steps: Describe a denomination where female priesthood is established: e.g. the Church of Sweden and several Protestant communities.
Describe a denomination where the office is reserved for men: e.g. the Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches.
Note that there are nonetheless internal voices and debates for change even within the more restrictive denominations.
Draw the conclusion that "the Christian view" is a simplification that obscures differences between and within denominations.
Formulate a more precise religious studies principle: always state which denomination, which community and which time a statement about a religion's view concerns.

questions.prompt: Summarise religion and gender roles, religious feminism, religion and sexual identity, and diversity of interpretation.
questions.opener: Go through the themes in turn: gender roles, feminism, sexual identity, diversity of interpretation.
questions.answer: Religion and gender roles: the view of gender varies between and within religious traditions and has changed historically in interplay with society — there is no single, clear-cut "religious view" of gender. Religious feminism: argues for equality based on the tradition's own sources, and often holds that unequal interpretations were shaped by historical, male-dominated interpretive traditions rather than by the sources themselves. Religion and sexual identity: great variation between and within traditions, from fully inclusive communities to more restrictive stances, often debated vigorously from within. Diversity of interpretation: the same religion can give rise to very different positions on questions such as female leadership or LGBTQ issues, depending on denomination, community and time period — a religious studies analysis should always specify which part of a tradition a statement concerns.
